documents.t: The example’s app.json includes the React Native Pay plugin (e.g. with a demo Merchant ID and Google Pay enabled). Change the plugin merchantIdentifier and any Google Pay runtime settings to your own for real payments.
Quick Start — Minimal integration in your app API: usePaymentCheckout — Hook options and return value Troubleshooting — Common integration issues and fixes

Decide which wallet button to show before the user taps anything. The library reports two flags, checked without blocking the JS thread: isSupported: the device can pay with Apple Pay or Google Pay, whether or not a card is set up. hasActiveCard: the user has a card ready on one of your supportedNetworks.

iOS Android isSupported PKPaymentAuthorizationViewController.canMakePayments(): hardware and parental controls allow Apple Pay isReadyToPay: Google Pay is available, and the user has a card or can add one hasActiveCard canMakePayments(usingNetworks:capabilities:) with your supportedNetworks and merchantCapabilities isReadyToPay with existingPaymentMethodRequired: true and your supportedNetworks, googlePayAllowedAuthMethods and merchantCapabilities Both flags are false when the check fails or, on Android, when Google Pay does not answer within 5 seconds. A value the payment would refuse rejects the payServiceStatus Promise with the configuration error that would fail startPayment: an unknown network, merchant capability or auth method, or a network list the platform offers none of (Google Pay has no idcredit or privateLabel). The hook logs the rejection and reports both flags as false.

On Android, the check goes to the Google Pay environment you pass as googlePayEnvironment, 'TEST' by default. In TEST, Google Pay answers hasActiveCard: true whether or not the user has a card (Google's reference), so a production app must pass 'PRODUCTION' to get real answers. An emulator with no Google account signed in answered false even in TEST, so test both signed-in and signed-out devices.
documents.s: Ask the environment you pay in

documents.t: Android: show the Google Pay button when isSupported is true. A user without a card adds one in the Google Pay sheet. Google offers no separate setup screen, so openPaymentSetup() does nothing on Android. iOS: show the Apple Pay buy button when hasActiveCard is true. When only isSupported is true, show the Set up Apple Pay button (buttonType="setUp") and call HybridPaymentHandler.openPaymentSetup() on tap. It opens Wallet (Settings on iPad) to add a card. Neither platform: when isSupported is false, hide the wallet buttons and offer another way to pay. In the example below, the checkout screen owns the hook and the cart, and WalletButton picks the button from the status. The user comes back from Wallet with a card the status does not know about yet, so the screen checks again when the app returns to the foreground: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { AppState, Button, Platform, View } from 'react-native' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, HybridPaymentHandler, usePaymentCheckout, type UsePaymentCheckoutReturn, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' export function CheckoutScreen() { const checkout = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', supportedNetworks: ['visa', 'mastercard'], // The environment you pay in, so the status is real in production. googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayGateway: 'stripe', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_stripe_merchant_id', }) const { refreshStatus } = checkout useEffect(() => { const subscription = AppState.addEventListener('change', (state) => { if (state === 'active') refreshStatus() }) return () => subscription.remove() }, [refreshStatus]) return ( <View> <Button title="Add Coffee" onPress={() => checkout.addItem('Coffee', '4.99')} /> {checkout.items.length > 0 && <WalletButton checkout={checkout} />} </View> ) } function WalletButton({ checkout }: { checkout: UsePaymentCheckoutReturn }) { const { isSupported, hasActiveCard, startPayment } = checkout // `isSupported` is `false` until the first check settles, and a refresh // keeps the last answer, so the button does not flicker on return. if (!isSupported) return null if (Platform.OS === 'android') { return ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" onPress={callback(startPayment)} /> ) } return hasActiveCard ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(startPayment)} /> ) : ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="setUp" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(() => HybridPaymentHandler.openPaymentSetup())} /> ) } The hook checks on mount, and again when supportedNetworks, merchantCapabilities or googlePayEnvironment change. isCheckingStatus is true while a check runs; the flags keep their last values until it settles.

HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus() returns a Promise. Pass the same networks, capabilities and environment as your payment request: import { HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const { isSupported, hasActiveCard } = await HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus({ supportedNetworks: ['visa', 'mastercard'], merchantCapabilities: ['3DS'], googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION', })
usePaymentCheckout: the hook's availability fields HybridPaymentHandler: payServiceStatus and openPaymentSetup Components: ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton
Ask the payer for an address, an email address or a phone number in the payment sheet, offer shipping methods, and read what they chose from the result.

Set any of these flags in the usePaymentCheckout config or in a PaymentRequest. Each flag fills one field of the result: Flag Result field iOS (Apple Pay) Android (Google Pay) billingContactRequired billingContact Billing name and postal address Full billing address of the card shippingContactRequired shippingContact Shipping name and postal address Full shipping address emailRequired emailAddress Email address Email address phoneNumberRequired phoneNumber Phone number Phone number, collected with an address (see below) A field is set only when you asked for it. Ask only for what you need to fulfil the order: each one is another step for the payer.

The details are in the result, and onAuthorize receives them as its second argument, so your server can check the address before it charges: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const order = { label: 'Coffee beans', total: '18.00' } // your order function useShippedOrder() { const { addItem, clearItems, startPayment } = usePaymentCheckout({ currencyCode: 'USD', shippingContactRequired: true, emailRequired: true, onAuthorize: async (token, { shippingContact, emailAddress }) => { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/orders', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token, shippingContact, emailAddress }), }) return response.ok ? { status: 'success' } : { status: 'failure', error: 'We cannot ship to this address' } }, }) useEffect(() => { addItem(order.label, order.total) return clearItems }, [addItem, clearItems]) return async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.status === 'success') { console.log('Shipping to', result.shippingContact?.postalAddress?.city) } } } With HybridPaymentHandler, set the same flags on the PaymentRequest; the details are in the PaymentResult and in startPayment(request, { onAuthorize }).

billingContact and shippingContact are PaymentContact objects: name: the full name, for example 'Jane Appleseed'. givenName, familyName: iOS only. Google Pay returns the name as one string. postalAddress: street (address lines joined with '\n'), city, state, postalCode, country (iOS only) and isoCountryCode (uppercase ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, such as 'US'). emailAddress and phoneNumber are plain strings. The phone number is in the format the payer entered. Parts the payer left empty are omitted, not empty strings.

Offer delivery options with shippingMethods. The hook doesn't take them, because its total only covers the cart, so build the request yourself and pass it to HybridPaymentHandler: import { HybridPaymentHandler, createPaymentRequest, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' async function payWithShipping() { const request = createPaymentRequest({ label: 'Coffee beans', amount: '18.00', currencyCode: 'USD', shippingContactRequired: true, shippingMethods: [ { identifier: 'standard', label: 'Standard', amount: '0.00', detail: '3–5 business days' }, { identifier: 'express', label: 'Express', amount: '7.50', detail: 'Next business day' }, ], }) const result = await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(request, { onAuthorize: async (token, { shippingMethod, shippingContact }) => { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/orders', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, // Your server prices the order from the method identifier, not the client's amount. body: JSON.stringify({ token, shipping: shippingMethod?.identifier, shippingContact }), }) return response.ok ? { status: 'success' } : { status: 'failure' } }, }) if (result.status === 'success') { console.log('Shipping with', result.shippingMethod?.label) } } The selected method is shown as its own line, labelled with its label, and included in the total. The total is your paymentItems plus the method's amount. The order matters. On iOS the first method is selected when the sheet opens, so put the default first. result.shippingMethod and the second argument of onAuthorize hold the selected entry of shippingMethods, as you sent it. Every identifier must be non-empty and unique, no amount may be negative, and the paymentItems must not total less than zero on their own: shipping can't make up for a larger discount. Otherwise the payment fails before the sheet opens, with code: 'CONFIGURATION' and an error such as Shipping method identifier "express" is used more than once. Android: Google Pay can't offer a choice yet (see below), so Android charges the first method: it appears as a line item, is included in the total and is returned as shippingMethod.

Phone number on Android: Google Pay only collects a phone number with an address. With shippingContactRequired, the phone number comes with the shipping address. Without it, Android asks for the phone number with the billing address, and asks for at least the billing name, country and postal code even when billingContactRequired is off. billingContact is still only set when you asked for it. Email and phone on iOS: Apple Pay returns them as part of the shipping contact, so the library requests them there. Without shippingContactRequired, no shipping address is requested. shippingType changes how Apple Pay labels the address, for example "Delivery Address" for 'delivery'. iOS only. See ShippingType.

Choosing a shipping method on Android: Google Pay only offers shipping options through its payment data callbacks, which need play-services-wallet 20. Until the library moves to it, Android charges the first method. Prices or shipping methods that depend on the address: while the sheet is open, the total only changes when the payer picks another shipping method on iOS. Limiting shipping countries: check the country on your server and resolve onAuthorize with 'failure'.
Use the cart API from usePaymentCheckout to add, update, and remove items before calling startPayment().

Single item: addItem('Product name', 29.99) addItem('Discount', -5, 'final') // negative for discounts Multiple items: addItems([ { label: 'Product', amount: 29.99 }, { label: 'Shipping', amount: 5 }, { label: 'Tax', amount: 2.8, type: 'final' }, ])
Change label or amount (or type) by index: updateItem(0, { label: 'Product (x2)', amount: 59.98 })
removeItem(index) // remove one item clearItems() // empty the cart

import { formatAmount, usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const { addItem, clearItems, total } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', }) // Add product with quantity const handleAddProduct = (name: string, unitPrice: number, quantity: number) => { // 1.1 * 3 is 3.3000000000000003; round it to the currency's decimals addItem(`${name} (×${quantity})`, formatAmount(unitPrice * quantity)) } // Apply percentage discount (a negative line item) const handleApplyDiscount = (percent: number) => { addItem('Discount', formatAmount(-total * (percent / 100)), 'final') } // Clear cart const handleClearCart = () => { clearItems() }

At least one item is required before startPayment(). Otherwise the hook sets an error and returns null. total is derived from items; you don’t set it manually. It is an exact decimal sum. Round computed amounts with formatAmount(value, currencyCode). startPayment() rejects amounts with more decimal places than the currency allows, which includes unrounded float results such as 1.1 * 3. See PaymentAmount. Discounts can be negative line items, as long as the total is not negative. Use type: 'final' for confirmed amounts (e.g. product price, tax); use 'pending' for estimates (e.g. shipping) if your flow supports it. One pending item makes the total an estimate. Google Pay shows the total as estimated (totalPriceStatus: 'ESTIMATED') and Apple Pay marks the total as pending. An estimate does not let you charge a different amount: Google Pay requires the amount you authorize and charge to match the totalPrice shown on the sheet, and a mismatch can be declined. If the final amount differs from the estimate, start a new payment with the final amount, unless your gateway explicitly supports adjusting it (for example, incremental authorization).
Use HybridPaymentHandler and createPaymentRequest when you want full control and do not need the hook’s cart state.

import { HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const status = await HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus({ supportedNetworks: ['visa', 'mastercard', 'amex'], googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION', }) if (!status.isSupported) { // Hide the pay button and show "Apple Pay / Google Pay not available" } Pass the same networks and Google Pay environment as the payment request in step 2. On iOS, when isSupported is true but hasActiveCard is false, you can show a Set up Apple Pay button instead; see Check availability.

Either use a helper or build the object yourself: import { createPaymentRequest, HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const paymentRequest = createPaymentRequest({ amount: 99.99, label: 'Premium Subscription', merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION', googlePayGateway: 'stripe', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_merchant_id', }) createPaymentRequest throws if the amount is invalid (see PaymentAmount). For multiple line items, build paymentItems yourself and pass the full PaymentRequest through normalizePaymentRequest, which applies the same checks. On iOS, the Merchant ID is read from the app entitlements unless you explicitly pass applePayMerchantIdentifier.

const handlePayment = async () => { try { const result = await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(paymentRequest) if (result.status === 'success' && result.token) { await sendTokenToServer(result.token, orderId) } else if (result.status === 'failed') { console.error('Payment failed:', result.code, result.error) } // 'cancelled': the user closed the sheet, nothing to report } catch (err) { console.error('Payment error:', err) } } To charge the token before the Apple Pay sheet closes, pass startPayment(paymentRequest, { onAuthorize }) and charge inside the callback instead of calling sendTokenToServer afterwards, so the token isn't charged twice. See Charge before the sheet closes.

Use the platform-specific button, and pass it status.isSupported from step 1 so it stays hidden when payments are unavailable. Its onPress must be wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, or the tap does nothing: import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' function PaymentButton({ isSupported, handlePayment, }: { isSupported: boolean handlePayment: () => Promise<void> }) { if (!isSupported) return null return Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="subscribe" theme="dark" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} /> ) }

One-off or fixed-amount payments (e.g. subscription, tip). You already have a cart elsewhere and only need to build a PaymentRequest once. You want to avoid the hook’s internal state. For cart-based checkout, usePaymentCheckout is usually simpler.
After a successful payment (result.status === 'success'), your app receives a token. Your backend must use this token with your payment gateway (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) to create the charge.

From the client, send at least: token — The full PaymentToken object (or the fields your gateway needs). Treat as sensitive. amount (and currency) — So the server can validate and charge the correct amount. Any order/cart id — So the server knows what was purchased, and as the base of your idempotency key. Don't key idempotency on PaymentResult.transactionId or token.transactionIdentifier. transactionId is deprecated: the device generates a new one for every successful result, so a retry gets a new key. transactionIdentifier is missing on Android. Example: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const order = { id: 'order_123', label: 'Premium plan', total: '49.99' } // your order function useOrderPayment() { const { addItem, clearItems, startPayment, total } = usePaymentCheckout({ currencyCode: 'USD', }) // Fill the cart before the user taps pay: startPayment() returns null // for an empty cart, and items added in the same handler arrive too late. useEffect(() => { addItem(order.label, order.total) return clearItems }, [addItem, clearItems]) // Pass this to the pay button's onPress, wrapped with callback(). return async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.status === 'success' && result.token) { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token: result.token, amount: total, currency: 'USD', orderId: order.id, }), }) if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Payment processing failed') } } }
documents.s: What to send to the server

documents.t: Without onAuthorize, Apple Pay shows its success checkmark as soon as the user authorizes, before your server has charged anything. If the charge then fails, the user has already seen "Done". Pass onAuthorize to charge the token while the sheet waits. Resolve with the outcome, and the sheet shows success or failure: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const order = { id: 'order_123', label: 'Premium plan', total: '49.99' } // your order function useOrderPayment() { const { addItem, clearItems, startPayment } = usePaymentCheckout({ currencyCode: 'USD', onAuthorize: async (token) => { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token, amount: order.total, currency: 'USD', orderId: order.id }), }) if (!response.ok) { const { error } = await response.json() return { status: 'failure', error } } return { status: 'success' } }, }) useEffect(() => { addItem(order.label, order.total) return clearItems }, [addItem, clearItems]) return async () => { const result = await startPayment() // result.status is 'success' only when onAuthorize returned 'success'. // The token is already charged, so don't send it to your server again. } } With HybridPaymentHandler, pass the same callback as startPayment(request, { onAuthorize }). The second argument of onAuthorize holds the contact details and shipping method the request asked for, such as the shipping address. See Shipping and contact details. How it behaves: Failure: { status: 'failure', error } makes the sheet show the failure state. startPayment resolves with status: 'failed', code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR' and your error. A rejected promise is treated the same way. Retries on iOS: if the user retries from the sheet after a failure or a timeout, onAuthorize runs again with the new token. The result reflects the last attempt. A retry can start while a timed-out charge is still running, so key idempotency on your order ID, not on the token. Timeout: onAuthorize must settle within 25 seconds (Apple Pay itself gives up after about 30). Otherwise the payment fails with code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR' and "Payment authorization timed out", and the late result is ignored. Your server may still have charged the card, so make the charge idempotent and reconcile by order ID. Android: Google Pay closes its sheet before it returns the token, and its basic flow has no step that waits for the merchant. onAuthorize still runs, with the same timeout, after the sheet closes, and its outcome decides the PaymentResult. The same callback works on both platforms.

Your backend receives the token and calls your gateway SDK/API. The exact request body and field mapping depend on your gateway + tokenization mode. Treat this example as shape guidance, not drop-in code. // Backend (Node.js example) app.post('/process-payment', async (req, res) => { const { token, amount, currency, orderId } = req.body try { // 1) Validate order/cart server-side (amount, currency, ownership, status) // 2) Choose gateway flow based on platform/gateway config // - iOS (Apple Pay): paymentData is Apple token payload (Base64 string) // - Android (Google Pay): paymentData is Google tokenization payload // 3) Call gateway API with the exact fields required by that provider // 4) Use idempotency keys and persist payment state const charge = await gateway.charge({ amountMinor: Math.round(amount * 100), currency, tokenPayload: token.paymentData, token: token, orderId, idempotencyKey: `charge-${orderId}`, }) res.json({ success: true, chargeId: charge.id }) } catch (err) { res.status(500).json({ error: err.message }) } }) Important: Use your gateway’s official docs for: Mapping PaymentToken fields to provider-specific request fields. Creating a payment method/source/intent from Apple Pay or Google Pay token payloads. Idempotency (e.g. a key derived from your order ID to avoid duplicate charges). Handling failures and refunds. Provider-specific walkthroughs in Przelewy24 Apple Pay + Google Pay cookbook.

Use HTTPS and authenticate the client (e.g. session or API key). Validate amount and currency on the server; do not trust the client for the charged amount. Do not log raw token payloads; treat them like card data. Prefer creating a PaymentIntent (or equivalent) on the server and confirming with the token, so the server controls the amount and idempotency.

Before you release, run a payment end to end on both platforms: in the Apple Pay sandbox on an iPhone, and in the Google Pay TEST environment on Android. This page covers both setups, the production access Google requires, and the flows to check before every release.

Only PRODUCTION with real cards proves that a charge goes through. Each test environment covers part of the flow: Environment Verifies Cannot verify iOS Simulator The sheet opens and shows your line items and the "Pay merchantName" total. Cancel, onAuthorize success and failure, and the double-tap guard. No card or account needed. A token your gateway can charge. Apple doesn't document what the Simulator's token contains, and developers report that its paymentData is empty. Apple also says the Simulator doesn't support every Apple Pay feature, without listing which. iPhone with a sandbox tester The full sheet with Apple's test cards, Face ID or passcode, and a token your payment processor can test decrypting. A completed charge. Apple says sandbox transactions are declined before fulfillment, because the test key doesn't match your production key. Android, TEST environment The Google Pay sheet with Google's test cards, the result handling, and onAuthorize. No Google Pay merchant ID needed. Availability: hasActiveCard is always true in TEST. A live charge: TEST tokens never carry real card data, so only your gateway's test environment can process them. Your production request: the merchant ID and the PRODUCTION checks only run in PRODUCTION. Android, PRODUCTION Everything, with real cards. Nothing. It needs production access first. Availability is hard to test on both platforms. On iOS, isSupported comes from PKPaymentAuthorizationViewController.canMakePayments(), which Apple documents as true when the device supports payments, even with no card in Wallet; hasActiveCard also needs a card on your networks. On Android, both flags come from the environment you pass as googlePayEnvironment, so only a PRODUCTION build shows real answers. See Check availability.

The Simulator runs the Apple Pay sheet without a card in Wallet or a sandbox account: npx expo run:ios Use it to check the sheet's contents and your app's handling of each result (see the release checklist). Don't send the Simulator's token to your gateway, and test anything that depends on a real token, such as your server's charge, on a device.

Apple's sandbox testing page lists the supported regions and the test card numbers. To run a sandbox payment: Create a sandbox tester. In App Store Connect, open Users and Access, then Sandbox, then Testers, and click +. Use an email address that isn't already an Apple Account. Sign the device in as the tester. On the iPhone, sign out of your Apple Account in Settings, then sign in with the sandbox tester. For Apple Pay the tester must be the device's Apple Account, not only the App Store's sandbox account. Set a supported region. In Settings → General → Language & Region, pick a region where Apple Pay sandbox is supported. Amex test cards only work with the UK or US region. Add a test card. In Wallet, tap +, choose a debit or credit card, and enter one of Apple's test cards manually. If Wallet asks for a verification code, enter 111111. Install a development build with Developer Mode on: npx expo run:ios --device The Merchant ID in your plugin config must belong to your Apple Developer team. The example app's Merchant ID (merchant.pl.sfd.sklep) won't sign with yours, so replace it before you run the example on a device. Pay. The sheet shows your test card. After you authorize, startPayment resolves with a sandbox token. What you do with the sandbox token depends on your gateway. Apple says your processor can use it to test decrypting the payment data, but the charge itself is declined. Some gateways don't take sandbox tokens at all: Stripe, for example, asks you to test with a real card in Wallet and its test API keys, and doesn't charge the card. Check your gateway's Apple Pay docs. Test cards only work in the sandbox, and real cards only work in production. Before release, sign the device back in to a regular Apple Account and pay once with a real card. If your gateway has a test mode for real cards, use it. If not, make a small charge and refund it.

Android uses the TEST environment unless you set googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION'. You need: A real device, or an emulator with a Google Play system image, signed in to a Google account. Google Wallet with a payment method. Google's setup page asks you to add one. Then run a development build: npx expo run:android In TEST, Google Pay shows a suite of test cards by default. You don't need to join anything. To see your account's real cards in TEST instead, join the googlepay-test-mode-real-data group. Real cards return placeholder data in TEST and are never charged. In TEST, the sheet always labels you as an unverified merchant. Get a token your gateway accepts. If you leave googlePayGateway and googlePayGatewayMerchantId empty in TEST, the library sends Google's example gateway with exampleGatewayMerchantId. Google says the example gateway returns no card data capable of a transaction, so your server can't charge it. To send a token to your gateway's test environment, set its test values: import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' usePaymentCheckout({ googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', googlePayGateway: 'your_gateway', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_test_gateway_merchant_id', }) Some gateways, such as Stripe, Braintree, and Adyen, show their own test cards in the sheet when the request carries their test parameters, and their test environment returns realistic responses. The library sends only gateway and gatewayMerchantId as tokenization parameters, so check your gateway's entry for the parameters it expects. What TEST can't verify: Availability. With existingPaymentMethodRequired, isReadyToPay always returns true in TEST, so hasActiveCard is true even with no card. An emulator with no Google account signed in answers false instead. You can't test the "no card" path of a signed-in user in TEST. A live charge. TEST tokens never carry real card data. With your gateway's test values, its test environment can process them, but nothing is charged. Your production request. The library sends googlePayMerchantId and requires googlePayMerchantId, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId only in PRODUCTION. A missing value fails with, for example, googlePayMerchantId is required in PRODUCTION, which you only see in a PRODUCTION build.

Google Pay only works in PRODUCTION after Google approves your app. Google's publishing guide has the full steps. In short: In the Google Pay & Wallet Console, choose the Merchant business type and complete your business profile. Open Google Pay API, then Get started, and accept the Google Pay API Terms of Service and Acceptable Use Policy. Your Google Pay merchant ID then appears in the Console. Pass it as googlePayMerchantId. Go through the integration checklist against your TEST build. Under Google Pay API → Integrations → Integrate with your Android app, pick your app and the Gateway integration type. The Console only lists apps published on Google Play under the same Google account. Upload screenshots of your TEST integration, and submit the app for approval. Once approved, set googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION' and your production gateway values, sign the app with your release key, and publish it on Google Play. Google says the debug key doesn't work in PRODUCTION. Until your app has production access, the sheet shows an "Unrecognized App" error. To find out why a PRODUCTION request fails, read the merchant error log: adb logcat -s WalletMerchantError Google's troubleshooting page lists the error codes, such as OR_BIBED_06 for the example gateway in production, and OR_BIBED_13 for a signing key that doesn't match.

Run these flows on an iPhone and on an Android device before every release, with the build configuration you ship. The example app's Simulated Server (onAuthorize) button rehearses them without a backend: tap it to cycle between off, approve, and decline. In approve and decline it waits 1.5 seconds and then resolves like a server that charged or declined the token. In your own app, use your server against your gateway's test mode, and your gateway's decline test cards or amounts for the decline flow. Success. Pay with a test card. startPayment resolves with status: 'success' and a token, and your server charges once. With onAuthorize, the Apple Pay sheet shows its checkmark only after your server answers. On Android, the Google Pay sheet closes first and onAuthorize runs after. User cancel. Open the sheet and close it without paying. startPayment resolves with status: 'cancelled' and code: 'CANCELLED'. Your server is not called. The hook leaves error as null, so your UI shows no failure. Decline through onAuthorize. Set the example app to decline, or make your server decline. On iOS, the sheet shows the failure and lets the user retry, which calls onAuthorize again with a new token. Closing the sheet resolves startPayment with status: 'failed', code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR' and your error. On Android, the sheet has already closed, and startPayment resolves with status: 'failed', code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR' and your error. The order isn't marked paid, and a retry doesn't charge twice. Make the charge idempotent per order ID, not per token. Slow server. Make your server take longer than 25 seconds to answer onAuthorize. startPayment resolves with code: 'PROVIDER_ERROR' and error: 'Payment authorization timed out'. On iOS, the user can first retry from the sheet. Your server may still charge after the app has given up. Check that your backend can reconcile that order. Double tap. Tap the pay button twice quickly. Only one sheet opens. The second call resolves at once with code: 'IN_PROGRESS', and the first payment settles normally. Your UI doesn't show the second result as a failed payment, and your server charges once. Backgrounding. Open the sheet, go to the home screen, and return to the app. Repeat after switching to another app. startPayment settles exactly once, isProcessing returns to false, and the next tap opens a new sheet. If the next payment reports code: 'IN_PROGRESS', or the app stays in its processing state, open an issue with the platform and OS version. Then check the release configuration: iOS: the Merchant ID in your plugin config is the one whose Payment Processing Certificate is installed in your gateway, and your server uses the gateway's live keys. Android: googlePayEnvironment is 'PRODUCTION', since an omitted value means TEST. googlePayMerchantId is your Console merchant ID, the gateway values are your live ones, Google has approved the app, and the build is signed with your release key. Both: merchantName is the business name you want on the sheet.

This cookbook shows how to use @gmisoftware/react-native-pay for wallet payments and process them with Przelewy24 on your backend. The library is not a gateway SDK. It only presents the native payment sheet and returns the payment token that your backend maps to Przelewy24 APIs. It follows the same contract used across this library: the app collects PaymentResult and PaymentToken the backend maps the token to Przelewy24 API calls

Przelewy24 REST docs (Apple Pay): developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 REST docs (Google Pay): developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 payment integration docs entry point: developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 mobile library docs (registration and verification concepts): GitHub README Use Przelewy24's official docs as the source of truth for provider request fields, signatures, endpoints, and enablement requirements.

Complete iOS (Apple Pay) setup: Apple Merchant ID Apple Pay capability enabled on your App ID Payment Processing Certificate Confirm your Przelewy24 account is configured for Apple Pay. Test on a real iOS device with Wallet configured.

Complete Android (Google Pay) setup: enableGooglePay: true (Expo plugin) Google Pay API enabled in Google Cloud gateway config in app code (googlePayMerchantId, googlePayEnvironment, googlePayGateway, googlePayGatewayMerchantId) Confirm your Przelewy24 account is configured for Google Pay. Test on a real device (or emulator with Google Play Services) and a wallet card.
Implement a backend endpoint that: accepts token payloads from app clients maps platform-specific token payloads to Przelewy24 fields verifies and persists payment status

App displays wallet button (ApplePayButton on iOS, GooglePayButton on Android). User confirms payment in the native sheet. App receives PaymentResult (status, token). App sends token + amount/currency/order data to backend over HTTPS. Backend calls Przelewy24 with platform-appropriate payload mapping. Backend verifies final status and returns checkout result to the app.

import React from 'react' import {ActivityIndicator, Platform, View} from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, usePaymentCheckout, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import {callback} from 'react-native-nitro-modules' export function CheckoutWithPrzelewy24() { const {startPayment, isSupported, isProcessing} = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'PL', currencyCode: 'PLN', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', // switch to PRODUCTION for live traffic googlePayGateway: 'przelewy24', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_przelewy24_gateway_merchant_id', }) const onPayPress = async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.status !== 'success' || !result.token) return await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/payments/przelewy24/wallet', { method: 'POST', headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({ platform: Platform.OS, // ios | android amount: 49.99, currency: 'PLN', orderId: 'order_123', token: result.token, }), }) } if (!isSupported) return null if (isProcessing) return <ActivityIndicator /> return ( <View> {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(onPayPress)} style={{width: '100%', height: 48}} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={4} onPress={callback(onPayPress)} style={{width: '100%', height: 48}} /> )} </View> ) }

Forward at least: token.paymentData (opaque payload; token format is platform/provider-dependent) order/cart identifier, which your backend also uses for idempotency amount and currency optional platform marker (ios / android) to simplify provider mapping Do not parse or transform paymentData in the client beyond forwarding it.

Provider field mapping must remain server-side. Keep this as an internal adapter and follow Przelewy24 docs for exact request schemas. app.post('/payments/przelewy24/wallet', async (req, res) => { const {platform, token, amount, currency, orderId} = req.body // 1) Validate amount/currency/order ownership server-side. // 2) Branch mapping by wallet platform. // 3) Build Przelewy24 request with required signatures/merchant fields. // 4) Persist payment status and return result. const p24Result = await przelewy24Client.createWalletPayment({ wallet: platform === 'ios' ? 'APPLE_PAY' : 'GOOGLE_PAY', amountMinor: Math.round(amount * 100), currency, orderId, // Not token.transactionIdentifier: it is missing on Android. idempotencyKey: `wallet-${orderId}`, walletTokenPayload: token?.paymentData, rawToken: token, }) res.json({success: true, providerPaymentId: p24Result.id}) })

Always use HTTPS between app and backend. Never log raw token payloads. Validate amount/currency/order ownership server-side. Use idempotency keys based on your order ID, not on transactionId or token.transactionIdentifier. Treat provider callbacks/webhooks and verification as the source of final payment state.

This package does not include a native Przelewy24 SDK adapter; integration is done through your backend. For production mapping and validation rules, rely on Przelewy24's official Apple Pay and Google Pay documentation.

React Native Pay is a unified payment module for React Native that supports Apple Pay (iOS) and Google Pay (Android) through a single, type-safe API for presenting native payment sheets and returning payment tokens.

One hook — usePaymentCheckout() handles availability, cart, and payment flow. Native buttons — ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton for platform-correct UI. Unified API — Shared request/result model across platforms; button component remains platform-specific. TypeScript — Full types and IntelliSense for requests, results, and tokens. Expo — Config plugin for Apple Pay entitlements and Google Pay metadata. Nitro Modules — High-performance native bindings.

React Native apps (Expo or bare) that need Apple Pay and/or Google Pay. Teams that want a single integration instead of maintaining two separate SDKs. Apps that already use (or plan to use) a payment gateway (e.g. Stripe, Braintree) and need the payment token from the device to charge on the server.

Check availability — isSupported and hasActiveCard from usePaymentCheckout() or HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus(). See Check availability. Build the cart — addItem() / addItems() (or build a PaymentRequest yourself). Show the button — ApplePayButton on iOS, GooglePayButton on Android. Start payment — startPayment(); user completes the sheet; you receive a token. Send token to server — Your backend uses the token with your payment gateway to complete the charge. The library does not process payments itself; it gives you the token and metadata so your server can.

Renders native payment buttons (ApplePayButton / GooglePayButton). Starts Apple Pay / Google Pay sheets and returns PaymentResult + token payload. Provides hook-based cart helpers (usePaymentCheckout) and low-level API (HybridPaymentHandler).
It does not charge cards by itself. It does not replace your gateway SDK/backend payment flow. It does not bypass Apple Developer / Google Pay onboarding and account setup.

Platform setup (Merchant ID, entitlements/capabilities, Google Pay API/project setup). Gateway configuration (environment, gateway identifiers, tokenization mode). Server-side processing (validation, idempotency, charge/intent creation, error handling). Real-device testing on iOS and Android before going live.
Quick Start — Get a minimal checkout running in minutes. Payment flow — End-to-end flow in more detail. Installation & Setup — Prerequisites and platform setup.
This page focuses on runtime behavior and integration boundaries so you can make your checkout resilient.

The library does not charge the user directly. It opens the native wallet sheet, returns a tokenized payment payload, and lets your backend complete the charge with your gateway. At a minimum: App checks wallet availability (isSupported / payServiceStatus()). App builds a PaymentRequest from cart items. User confirms payment in the native sheet. App receives PaymentResult (status, code, token). Backend validates order context and charges through your provider.

sequenceDiagram actor User participant App participant NativeSheet participant Backend participant Gateway App->>App: Build paymentRequest from cart App->>NativeSheet: startPayment(paymentRequest) User->>NativeSheet: Confirm or cancel NativeSheet-->>App: PaymentResult(status, code, token) alt success with token App->>Backend: POST token + amount + currency + orderId Backend->>Backend: Validate order state and idempotency Backend->>Gateway: Create charge/intent using token Gateway-->>Backend: Authorized or failed Backend-->>App: Final checkout status else status cancelled App->>App: Stay on checkout, no error else status failed App->>App: Handle result.code end

With onAuthorize, your backend charges the token before startPayment resolves: on iOS while the Apple Pay sheet is still up, on Android after the Google Pay sheet has closed. The result below already reflects the charge, so don't send result.token to your backend again. Every result has a status. When it isn't 'success', code says why: status success code What to do 'success' true none Forward result.token to your backend, unless onAuthorize already charged it. Wait for your backend before marking the order paid. 'cancelled' false 'CANCELLED' The user closed the sheet. Leave the checkout as it was and don't show an error. 'failed' false any other code See the table below. Neither platform rejects the startPayment promise for these outcomes. error is a message for your logs, and it is also set on a cancel ('Payment cancelled by user'). Branch on status and code, not on the message. import type { PaymentResult } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' function describeOutcome(result: PaymentResult): string | null { switch (result.status) { case 'success': return null case 'cancelled': return null // the user closed the sheet case 'failed': switch (result.code) { case 'IN_PROGRESS': return null // the payment already in flight will settle case 'NOT_AVAILABLE': return 'Apple Pay / Google Pay is not available. Choose another payment method.' case 'PROVIDER_ERROR': return 'The payment did not go through. Try again or choose another payment method.' default: return 'Something went wrong. Please try again later.' } } }

code Meaning Where it comes from What to do 'CANCELLED' The sheet closed before the user authorized. iOS: the sheet closed without an authorization. PassKit doesn't say why, so a sheet that closes by itself also reports a cancel (see Troubleshooting). Android: the sheet returned RESULT_CANCELED, also when the user dismisses Google's sign-in prompt, or a Google Pay error has CANCELED / ERROR_CODE_USER_CANCELLED. Nothing. Don't show an error. 'IN_PROGRESS' Another payment is still in flight. No sheet was shown. Both: startPayment called while a payment hasn't settled (see isPaymentInProgress()). Ignore it. The payment in flight settles normally. 'CONFIGURATION' The request or the app's setup is invalid. Retrying won't help. Both: an invalid amount, a negative total, an unknown merchant capability, invalid shippingMethods, and supportedNetworks that is empty, has an unknown name or has no network the platform offers. iOS: no Apple Pay merchant ID, an unknown shippingType. Android: more than two decimal places, an unknown googlePayAllowedAuthMethods value, PRODUCTION without googlePayMerchantId, googlePayGateway or googlePayGatewayMerchantId, and a Google Pay error with DEVELOPER_ERROR, ERROR_CODE_INVALID_PARAMETERS, ERROR_CODE_MERCHANT_ACCOUNT_ERROR or ERROR_CODE_UNSUPPORTED_API_VERSION. Fix the request or the setup; error says what is wrong. Show the user a generic error. 'NOT_AVAILABLE' The device can't show the payment sheet right now. iOS: PassKit can't create the sheet, which Apple documents for a user who can't pay with any of the request's networks, or there is no active window to present it from. Android: no current activity, the Google Pay sheet fails to start, and a Google Pay error with SIGN_IN_REQUIRED, API_NOT_CONNECTED, ERROR_CODE_BUYER_ACCOUNT_ERROR or ERROR_CODE_AUTHENTICATION_FAILURE. Offer another payment method. Show the pay button only as Check availability describes, from isSupported and hasActiveCard. 'PROVIDER_ERROR' Apple Pay, Google Pay or your onAuthorize reported a failure. Both: onAuthorize resolved with 'failure', rejected, or didn't settle within 25 seconds. Android: any other Google Pay error, such as a network or internal error, and payment data that is missing or can't be read. Let the user retry or choose another payment method. After a timeout, your server may still have charged: reconcile the order. 'UNKNOWN' Anything else. iOS: an unexpected error while starting the payment. Android: an unexpected result code or exception, or a Google Pay error without a status. Show a generic error and log error. A Google Pay error arrives either from loadPaymentData or as the sheet's RESULT_ERROR; both are mapped the same way, and its status code is added to error, for example Payment error: <message> (status code 10).
startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout returns null when an exception occurs, and sets error. Handle this as an app/runtime failure path (show generic error + retry).

Calling startPayment() with no cart items returns null and sets a "Cart is empty" error. An invalid amount or a negative total also returns null and sets error, without opening the sheet. Gate the pay button on items.length > 0.

PaymentToken.paymentData is an opaque gateway payload and is platform/gateway-dependent: Apple Pay (iOS): Base64-encoded data from the Apple Pay token payload. Google Pay (Android): Tokenization payload from Google Pay (tokenizationData.token), whose schema depends on your configured gateway. Always send the entire token object (or exactly the fields your gateway asks for) to your backend. Avoid parsing or transforming token payloads in the client.

Your backend should: Validate order ownership, amount, and currency from server-side order data. Use an idempotency key derived from your order ID to prevent duplicate charges. Don't use PaymentResult.transactionId: the device generates a new one for every result. Call gateway APIs with the provider-specific token mapping. Persist both wallet result and gateway result for audit/debug. Return a final, app-friendly checkout status.

iOS: Merchant ID and Payment Processing Certificate set up and installed in your gateway. Android: Google Pay API enabled; production gateway merchant ID and environment configured. Backend: Endpoint validates the token, amount, and context and uses the gateway SDK to create the charge. Security: Never log or expose raw token payloads; use HTTPS and secure storage for any sensitive data. Next: API: usePaymentCheckout or Server-side processing.
Get a minimal Apple Pay / Google Pay checkout running in your app.

Use the hook and the platform-specific button. On press, call startPayment() and send the token to your server. import React from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout, ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, formatAmount, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { Platform, View, Text, Button, ActivityIndicator } from 'react-native' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' function CheckoutScreen() { const { isSupported, isCheckingStatus, items, total, addItem, addItems, removeItem, startPayment, isProcessing, error, } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', }) const handlePay = async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.status === 'success' && result.token) { // Send result.token to your backend await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token: result.token, orderId: 'order_123', // your order }), }) } } if (isCheckingStatus) { return <View><ActivityIndicator /></View> } if (!isSupported) { return <View><Text>Apple Pay / Google Pay is not available</Text></View> } return ( <View style={{ padding: 20 }}> <Button title="Add Coffee ($4.99)" onPress={() => addItem('Coffee', 4.99)} /> {items.map((item, i) => ( <View key={i} style={{ flexDirection: 'row', padding: 10 }}> <Text>{item.label}: ${formatAmount(item.amount)}</Text> <Button title="Remove" onPress={() => removeItem(i)} /> </View> ))} <Text style={{ fontSize: 20, marginVertical: 10 }}>Total: ${total.toFixed(2)}</Text> {error && <Text style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {error.message}</Text>} {isProcessing ? ( <ActivityIndicator size="large" /> ) : ( Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePay)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={4} onPress={callback(handlePay)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} /> ) )} </View> ) } If you are integrating with Przelewy24, follow the provider cookbook: Przelewy24.

ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton are Nitro views, so their onPress must be wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, as in the screen above. A bare function does not reach the native button, and tapping it does nothing. See Troubleshooting: Nitro callback for onPress.

iOS: Real device with a card in Wallet; Simulator has limited support. Android: Real device or emulator with Google Play Services; add a card in Google Pay. For Google Pay, configure googlePayMerchantId, googlePayEnvironment, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId when you move to a real gateway (see Android setup and API: usePaymentCheckout).

react-native-nitro-modules and @gmisoftware/react-native-pay installed. Native config done (Expo plugin + prebuild, or bare iOS entitlements + Android manifest). Checkout screen uses usePaymentCheckout and the platform-specific button. Apple and/or Google account/platform configuration is complete. Backend endpoint validates order amount/currency and processes the token with your gateway. Idempotency and retry handling are implemented server-side. Real-device tests passed on iOS and Android. Next: Payment flow or Installation & Setup.
Configure your app and Google Pay for Android.

In app.json (or app.config.js), enable Google Pay: { "expo": { "plugins": [ ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "enableGooglePay": true }] ] } } Use the same plugin with merchantIdentifier if you also support iOS.
In Google Cloud Console, open your project. Enable the Google Pay API for the project. For production, Google must also approve your app in the Google Pay & Wallet Console. See Production access.

Google Pay needs a Google Pay merchant ID for production, plus your payment gateway details (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) and gateway merchant ID. Configure them in usePaymentCheckout (or in your PaymentRequest): import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', // shown on the Google Pay sheet currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', // or 'PRODUCTION' googlePayGateway: 'stripe', // or braintree, square, adyen, etc. googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_stripe_merchant_id', }) If you omit merchantName, the Google Pay sheet shows your app's label (android:label in the manifest). Supported gateways include: stripe, braintree, square, adyen, authorizenet, checkoutltd. See Google Pay Gateway Tokens for the full list and exact identifiers.
npx expo prebuild --clean npx expo run:android

Use a real device or an emulator with a Google Play system image, signed in to a Google account. In googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', Google Pay shows its test cards, and no token can be used for a live charge. See TEST environment for what it can't verify and how to get a token your gateway accepts. PRODUCTION needs Google's approval. See Production access. Before each release, run the release checklist.

If the user switches to another app while the Google Pay sheet is open, Android can kill your app's process to free memory. When the user comes back and finishes or closes the sheet, your app restarts with a new JS runtime. The startPayment() call that opened the sheet no longer exists, so its result is dropped: No token reaches your app, so your backend charges nothing. The cart and checkout screen are gone unless your app restores them. The user has to start the payment again. The payment survives a recreated Activity, for example after a configuration change your Activity doesn't handle: the result still reaches startPayment(). To reproduce a process death, open the sheet, press Home, run adb shell am kill <your.package.name>, reopen the app from Recents, and close the sheet.

The @gmisoftware/react-native-pay Expo config plugin configures native projects so Apple Pay and Google Pay work without manual edits.
Add the plugin to app.json or app.config.js: { "expo": { "plugins": [ [ "@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.yourcompany.app", "enableGooglePay": true } ] ] } }

Option Type Description merchantIdentifier string or string[] Apple Pay Merchant ID(s). If omitted, Apple Pay entitlements are not added. enableGooglePay boolean If true, adds the Google Pay metadata to the Android manifest. Default: false.

iOS only (Apple Pay): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.example.app" }] Android only (Google Pay): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "enableGooglePay": true }] Both platforms: ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.example.app", "enableGooglePay": true }] Multiple Merchant IDs (iOS): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": ["merchant.com.example.app", "merchant.com.example.other"], "enableGooglePay": true }]

documents.t: In the Merchant ID page, create a Payment Processing Certificate. Follow Apple’s steps (CSR, etc.) and download the certificate. Install it in your payment processor (e.g. Stripe, Braintree) as per their docs. The library does not process payments; your gateway uses this certificate to validate tokens. Apple Pay shows the total as "Pay merchant". Pass your business name as merchantName: import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', }) The sheet lists your cart items and then the total line "Pay Your Store", which the library adds for you. If you omit merchantName, the total uses your app's display name (CFBundleDisplayName).

The iOS Simulator shows the Apple Pay sheet without a card, but its token can't be charged. See what the Simulator can't verify. On an iPhone, test with an Apple Pay sandbox tester and Apple's test cards. See Sandbox on an iPhone. Before each release, run the release checklist.

Button not showing / “Cannot make payments”: Ensure Merchant ID matches exactly, entitlements are present after prebuild, and the device has Wallet & Apple Pay set up with a valid card. See Troubleshooting for more.
Common issues and fixes for React Native Pay.

Ensure your cart is not empty. startPayment() returns null with a "Cart is empty" error when items.length === 0. Test on a real device whenever possible (simulator/emulator payment support is limited). Re-run native generation after plugin changes: npx expo prebuild --clean

startPayment doesn't throw for a declined, cancelled or misconfigured payment. It resolves with a PaymentResult whose status and code say how it ended; Error codes explains each code. When debugging: Read error: it names the problem, and on Android it ends with Google Pay's status code. Branch on code in your app, though: the text may change. A 'CANCELLED' you didn't cause by closing the sheet usually points to setup. See The Apple Pay sheet closes right away and Cancelled on a device without a Google account.

On React Native 0.80+ (e.g. Expo SDK 57), the app can abort at startup with a stack ending in folly::dynamic::get<bool>() / BaseViewProps. Linking the library is enough; no pay button needs to be on screen. Cause: NitroPay.podspec defined FOLLY_NO_CONFIG, mismatching React Native core's folly config. Fixed after 0.0.16 — upgrade, then rebuild: npx expo prebuild --clean

documents.t: Merchant ID mismatch: The Expo plugin merchantIdentifier must exactly match your Apple Developer Merchant ID. Missing entitlement/capability: Confirm "Apple Pay Payment Processing" is enabled in Xcode and linked to the same Merchant ID. Wrong device context: Prefer a real iPhone with Wallet configured.

Add a valid card in Settings -> Wallet & Apple Pay. Confirm the App ID has Apple Pay enabled and linked to your Merchant ID. For production, ensure your Payment Processing Certificate is created and installed in your gateway.
documents.s: "Cannot make payments" or payment sheet fails

documents.t: startPayment resolves with status: 'cancelled' whenever the sheet closes before the user authorizes. PassKit doesn't tell the app why the sheet closed, so a sheet that closes by itself, or barely appears, reports the same cancel. One reported cause is a merchant ID that Apple Pay isn't set up for: The merchant ID in the request, or the first one in your app's entitlements, must be listed under the Apple Pay Payment Processing capability in Xcode and in your App ID. Rebuild after changing the Expo plugin's merchantIdentifier: npx expo prebuild --clean. See Apple Pay button not showing for the full checklist.
documents.s: The Apple Pay sheet closes right away

documents.t: The payment fails with code: 'CONFIGURATION' and Unknown merchant capability "<value>". Use "3DS", "EMV", "Credit" or "Debit" when merchantCapabilities contains any other value, on Android too. Case doesn't matter ('3ds' works). See MerchantCapability.

Use only supported Apple button values: buttonType: 'buy' | 'setUp' | 'book' | 'donate' | 'continue' | 'reload' | 'addMoney' | 'topUp' | 'order' | 'rent' | 'support' | 'contribute' | 'tip' buttonStyle: 'white' | 'whiteOutline' | 'black'

Set enableGooglePay: true in your Expo plugin config. Ensure Google Play Services is available (real device or Play-enabled emulator). Render only the Android button on Android (Platform.OS === 'android').
Add at least one card in Google Pay on the device. Use googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST' for test flows. Verify googlePayMerchantId, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId.

The check asked the Google Pay TEST environment, which reports a card whether or not there is one. Pass googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION' to usePaymentCheckout or payServiceStatus. An emulator with no Google account signed in reports false even in TEST. See Check availability.

documents.t: Google Pay asks the user to sign in to a Google account before it shows the sheet. Dismissing that prompt returns the same result as closing the sheet, so startPayment resolves with status: 'cancelled'. Sign in to a Google account on the device or emulator, and add a card to it.

documents.t: When Google Pay reports a setup problem, such as DEVELOPER_ERROR, the result has code: 'CONFIGURATION' and Google's status code at the end of error (for example (status code 10)). Google logs the details of merchant setup problems to logcat: adb logcat -s WalletMerchantError The OR_BIBED_* codes there are explained on Google's troubleshooting page, such as OR_BIBED_06 for the example gateway in production.
Run npx expo prebuild --clean and rebuild. Ensure no other plugin overrides Google Pay metadata in AndroidManifest.xml.

The library writes to logcat in debug builds only. Release builds log nothing, because the payment request holds your merchant IDs, item labels and amounts. To see the logs, run a debug build and filter by tag: adb logcat -s HybridPaymentHandler HybridGooglePayButton Payment errors don't depend on logs: they reach your app in result.error.

ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton are Nitro views. Nitro passes a function prop to native code only when it is wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, so onPress must always be wrapped. A bare function does not reach the native button: tapping it does nothing, and TypeScript reports Type '() => Promise<void>' is not assignable to type 'NitroViewWrappedCallback<...>'. import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const handlePay = async () => { // Call startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout here } {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePay)} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" onPress={callback(handlePay)} /> )} Use this pattern anywhere you pass handlers to ApplePayButton or GooglePayButton.
Install react-native-nitro-modules (required): bun add react-native-nitro-modules. Rebuild after adding/upgrading the package.
